scenes.visual: title card: Selection Has an Agent

scenes.tts: Natural selection starts with variants that already exist. Something in the environment, a predator, a parasite, a rival, a choosy mate, a drought, makes some of those variants leave more offspring than others. That difference in reproductive success is selection. It happens within one generation. It becomes evolution only if the variation is inherited, so that the young of the survivors resemble them. And if the environment changes, a different variant can win.
scenes.visual: row of varied individuals; an agent icon (bird, wasp, rival, female, sun for drought) sorts them; two-step strip: 'selection: one generation' then 'response: needs inheritance'

scenes.tts: Take the peppered moth. It comes in a pale form and a dark form, and the colour is inherited. Birds hunt the moths by sight on tree trunks. Where pollution killed the lichens and coated the bark with soot, dark moths matched the bark, and the dark form became common around industrial cities. When the air cleaned up and the lichens came back, pale moths matched better, and the dark form declined. Same moth, same birds. A different environment favoured a different colour.
scenes.visual: two trunks side by side, sooty and lichen-covered; pale and dark moth dots on each; a bird takes the conspicuous one on each trunk

scenes.tts: How do you show it? Michael Majerus released live moths of both forms near Cambridge over six years and recorded which disappeared, presumed eaten by birds. Cook and colleagues analysed his records. Each day, a dark moth survived at about zero point nine one times the rate of a pale one. That number is relative, and per day, at one site. It is a measured fitness component, survival, with a named agent, birds.
scenes.visual: release map dot near Cambridge; label 'dark survival = 0.91 x pale, per day, one site'; tags 'fitness component: survival' and 'agent: birds'

scenes.tts: Selection also has a shape. Plot fitness against a trait. Goldenrod gall flies are caught between two enemies. Wasps take the larvae in small galls, and birds open the large ones, so middle sized galls survive best. That is stabilizing selection. In crowded lake enclosures, sticklebacks at either extreme of a trait scored better on stand ins for how many young they could make than fish in the middle. That is disruptive selection, and crowding made it stronger.
scenes.visual: fitness-versus-gall-size curve peaking in the middle, wasp on the left slope, bird on the right; then a curve that dips in the middle, deeper for the high-density enclosure

scenes.tts: Sometimes the winner depends on how common it is. In Trinidad streams, researchers made one colour pattern of male guppy rare in some pools and common in others. Whichever pattern was rare had better estimated survival. And selection can act through mating. Malte Andersson shortened and lengthened the tails of male widowbirds in Kenya. Males given longer tails attracted more females to nest on their territories.
scenes.visual: two pools with three common and one rare guppy, roles reversed, rare one ringed; then three widowbirds with short, normal and long tails and nest counts rising left to right

scenes.tts: Each of these studies measured selection within one generation. None of them, by itself, shows evolution. For that, the trait must be inherited, so that the next generation carries more of the favoured variant. A drought does not create deep beaks. It removes more of the shallow ones. Selection sorts what is already there, and inheritance carries the sorting forward.
scenes.visual: a sieve sorting beak shapes; arrow to the next generation labelled 'only if inherited'
